title: Reflection (reflect)
summary: **Reflection** lets a Go program inspect and manipulate values whose types it doesn't know at compile time. The `reflect` package exposes a value's `Type` and `Value` at runtime — powering encoding/json, ORMs, and dependency-injection frameworks — at the cost of speed, safety, and clarity, so you reach for it sparingly.

subtopics.title: reflect.Type and reflect.Value
subtopics.explanation: reflect.TypeOf(x) returns a reflect.Type describing x's static type; reflect.ValueOf(x) returns a reflect.Value wrapping the data. Type answers 'what is it?' (name, kind, fields, methods); Value lets you read and, if settable, write the actual data.

subtopics.title: Kind vs Type
subtopics.explanation: Type is the named type (e.g. time.Duration); Kind is the underlying category (Int64, Struct, Ptr, Slice...). Switch on Kind to handle the shape of data generically; check Type when you care about the specific named type.

subtopics.title: Settability and addressability
subtopics.explanation: reflect can only modify a value that is *settable* — meaning it was obtained through a pointer and is addressable. reflect.ValueOf(x) gives an unaddressable copy; you need reflect.ValueOf(&x).Elem() to mutate the original.

subtopics.title: Reading struct tags
subtopics.explanation: Field metadata like `json:"name,omitempty"` is read via Type.Field(i).Tag.Get("json"). This is how encoding/json, validators, and ORMs map struct fields to external names without code generation.

subtopics.title: The interface type-value pair
subtopics.explanation: An interface value is internally a (type, value) pair. reflect works by unpacking that pair from an interface{}. This is why reflect.TypeOf takes interface{}: the type information rides along inside the interface header.

subtopics.title: Calling methods dynamically
subtopics.explanation: Value.MethodByName("Foo").Call(args) invokes a method found at runtime, passing a []reflect.Value of arguments and getting back results as []reflect.Value. This powers RPC dispatch and plugin systems, but it bypasses compile-time checks.

foundations.overview: Most Go code knows its types at compile time. But some code — a JSON encoder, a database mapper, a generic printer — must work with values whose types it can't know in advance. Reflection is the runtime mechanism that makes this possible: given any value via an interface{}, the reflect package reveals its type, kind, fields, tags, and methods, and (carefully) lets you read and write it. It's powerful and necessary, but slow and easy to misuse, so idiomatic Go treats it as a specialist tool, not an everyday one.
foundations.formalDefinition: Reflection is the ability of a program to examine and modify its own structure and behavior at runtime. In Go it is provided by the reflect package, which operates on the (type, value) pair stored inside an interface, exposing reflect.Type and reflect.Value handles.
foundations.whyItMatters: Reflection is the engine behind the standard library's encoding packages (json, xml, gob), ORMs (GORM), validators, and DI/wiring frameworks. Understanding it explains how those libraries work, and lets you build generic tooling when generics aren't enough.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an interface value as a sealed parcel with a shipping label: the label (type) says what's inside and the box (value) holds the data. Reflection is opening the parcel at runtime to read the label and inspect the contents — and, only if you were handed the parcel by reference, to repack it with something new.
foundations.runtimePerspective: An interface{} is two machine words: a pointer to type metadata (itab/type descriptor) and a pointer to the data. reflect.TypeOf reads the first word; reflect.ValueOf wraps the second. Because every reflective operation goes through these descriptors and dynamic dispatch — not direct field offsets — it is far slower than the equivalent static code and allocates more.
foundations.realWorldUsage: encoding/json marshaling arbitrary structs, ORMs mapping rows to struct fields by tag, validation libraries enforcing rules declared in tags, and frameworks injecting dependencies by inspecting constructor signatures.
foundations.businessImpact: Reflection-based libraries eliminate mountains of hand-written boilerplate (no manual JSON codecs per type), accelerating delivery — though hot paths often later replace reflection with code generation to recover speed.
foundations.engineeringImpact: It enables generic, declarative APIs, but errors move from compile time to runtime (panics), so reflective code needs careful guards and thorough tests.
foundations.performanceImpact: Reflective field access and method calls are an order of magnitude slower than static access and allocate; high-throughput systems cache reflect.Type info or switch to code generation (e.g. easyjson) for hot paths.
commonUseCases: Mapping struct tags to DB columns or config keys
Validation rules declared in struct tags
Dynamic method dispatch in RPC/plugin systems

commonMisconceptions.reality: It wraps a copy and is unaddressable. To mutate the original you must pass a pointer: reflect.ValueOf(&x).Elem(), which is settable.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Kind and Type are the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Kind is the underlying category (Int, Struct, Ptr); Type is the specific named type. time.Duration has Type 'time.Duration' but Kind Int64.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Reflection is just a clever trick with no cost.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Every reflective op uses dynamic dispatch and often allocates; it's roughly an order of magnitude slower than static code.

visualExplorer.caption: reflect unpacks the two words of an interface: a pointer to the type descriptor (read by TypeOf) and a pointer to the data (wrapped by ValueOf). That pair is the foundation of all reflection.

config.intro: What encoding/json does, conceptually, via reflect:

steps.name: Unpack the interface
steps.detail: reflect.ValueOf(v) and reflect.TypeOf(v) extract the value and type from the interface{} you passed in.

steps.name: Check the Kind
steps.detail: If Kind is Ptr, call Elem() to dereference; then confirm Kind == Struct before ranging fields.

steps.name: Iterate fields
steps.detail: For i in 0..NumField(): Type.Field(i) gives the field's name and StructTag; Value.Field(i) gives its data.

steps.name: Read the tag
steps.detail: Field(i).Tag.Get("json") tells the encoder the external key name and options like omitempty.

steps.name: Emit
steps.detail: The field's reflect.Value is converted (Interface()) and written out — recursing for nested structs/slices.

interactiveExamples.title: Inspect a struct's fields and tags
interactiveExamples.explanation: This is the core of how encoding/json works. We get the Type, range its exported fields, and read each field's value and json tag. Note Kind (Struct) vs the named Type (main.User).

code.expectedOutput:
type: main.User kind: struct
Name = Ada (json:"name")
Age = 36 (json:"age,omitempty")

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: make the value settable so we can mutate it
interactiveExamples.explanation: reflect.ValueOf(x) wraps a copy and panics if you try to Set it. Pass a POINTER and call .Elem() to get an addressable, settable Value. Fix the code so x becomes 99.

interactiveExamples.title: Call a method by name at runtime
interactiveExamples.explanation: MethodByName looks up a method on the value and Call invokes it with a slice of reflect.Value arguments. This is how RPC frameworks dispatch to handlers. The results come back as []reflect.Value.

checkpoints.prompt: What does this print for a time.Duration value?
checkpoints.explanation: Type is the specific named type, time.Duration. Kind is the underlying category, which for Duration is int64. This Type-vs-Kind distinction is central to reflection: switch on Kind for shape, check Type for identity.

checkpoints.prompt: This is supposed to set the field to 42 but panics at runtime. Why?
options: ValueOf(u) is an unaddressable copy, so its fields aren't settable
checkpoints.explanation: reflect.ValueOf(u) wraps a copy of u; it isn't addressable, so any Set on it (or its fields) panics. Pass a pointer: reflect.ValueOf(&u).Elem().FieldByName("Age").SetInt(42), and the field must be exported.

checkpoints.prompt: Why can't reflect set an *unexported* struct field even via a pointer?
options: Unexported fields don't exist at runtime
It would break package encapsulation, so reflect marks them non-settable (CanSet is false)
You must use unsafe for any field
checkpoints.explanation: reflect deliberately refuses to Set unexported fields (CanSet returns false) to preserve package encapsulation; you can read them with care but not write them through the normal API. Always guard with CanSet() before calling Set.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the call so v wraps an addressable, settable value of x.
checkpoints.explanation: reflect.ValueOf(&x) wraps the pointer; .Elem() dereferences it to the addressable value x points at, which is settable. reflect.ValueOf(x) would wrap an unaddressable copy and SetInt would panic.

codeLab.title: Apply default values from struct tags
codeLab.instructions: Implement `SetDefaults(ptr interface{})` that, for a pointer to a struct, fills any *zero-valued* exported field whose `default:"..."` tag is set. Support string and int fields. Use reflect: dereference the pointer, range fields, check IsZero(), read the tag, and Set the parsed value. The harness verifies via a reflect-based test.
hints: Reject anything that isn't a non-nil pointer; you can only mutate the original through a pointer.
Call .Elem() to get the addressable struct, then NumField()/Field(i) to iterate.
Use Tag.Lookup("default") (not Get) so you can tell 'no tag' from an empty default.
Only overwrite when CanSet() && IsZero() so already-set fields are preserved.

debuggingLab.title: Mutation silently does nothing (or panics)
debuggingLab.symptom: A function meant to populate a struct via reflection either panics with 'using unaddressable value' or leaves the caller's struct unchanged.

brokenCode.expectedOutput: panic: reflect: reflect.Value.SetString using unaddressable value

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Two layers of the same mistake: u is passed by value (so even a successful mutation wouldn't reach the caller), and reflect.ValueOf wraps an unaddressable copy (so Set panics). To mutate the caller's struct you must pass &u and reflect through .Elem() to reach the addressable original.
commonMistakes: Passing a struct by value and expecting reflective mutation to persist.
Calling Set on reflect.ValueOf(x) instead of reflect.ValueOf(&x).Elem().
Forgetting to guard with CanSet() (also catches unexported fields).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Pass a pointer and reflect through Elem(), guarding with CanSet().

theory.question: Explain the difference between reflect.Type and reflect.Value, and between Type and Kind.
theory.directAnswer: reflect.Type describes a value's type — its name, kind, fields, and methods — while reflect.Value wraps the actual data so you can read it and, if settable, write it. Kind is the underlying category (Int, Struct, Ptr, Slice...); Type is the specific named type. For example time.Duration has Kind Int64 but Type 'time.Duration'. You switch on Kind to handle shape generically and check Type for a specific named type.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two complementary handles obtained from the (type, value) pair inside an interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Generic code needs to ask both 'what shape is this?' (Kind) and 'what exactly is it?' (Type), and to read/write the data (Value).
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: TypeOf reads the interface's type word; ValueOf wraps its data word; Kind() collapses many named types to their underlying category.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing Type and Kind, or Type and Value, is the most common reflection mistake.
theory.realWorldExample: encoding/json switches on Kind (Struct, Slice, Map) to decide how to encode, but uses Type to find struct tags.

followUps.question: Why does TypeOf take an interface{}?
followUps.answer: Because the type information is carried inside the interface's (type, value) pair; passing through interface{} is how reflect receives both.

followUps.question: How do you get from a reflect.Value back to an ordinary value?
followUps.answer: Call v.Interface() to get an interface{}, then type-assert it.

theory.question: What does it mean for a reflect.Value to be settable, and what are the rules?
theory.directAnswer: A Value is settable only if it is addressable and was not obtained from an unexported field. reflect.ValueOf(x) wraps a copy and is never settable; to mutate the original you must wrap a pointer and call .Elem(), e.g. reflect.ValueOf(&x).Elem(). Even then, unexported struct fields remain non-settable to preserve encapsulation. Always guard with CanSet() before calling Set.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The runtime permission to write through a reflect.Value.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Reflection must not violate Go's value semantics (you can't mutate a copy) or its export rules.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Addressability comes from a pointer/Elem chain; export status comes from the field name's case; CanSet reports both.

theory.whyImportant: Settability is the #1 source of reflection panics in real code.
theory.realWorldExample: A config loader takes &cfg and reflects through Elem() so it can write fields decoded from env vars.

followUps.question: How do you create a brand-new settable value of a type?
followUps.answer: reflect.New(t) returns a pointer Value to a fresh zero value; .Elem() gives the settable value.

followUps.question: Can you read unexported fields even if you can't set them?
followUps.answer: You can observe them, but Interface() panics for unexported fields; reading raw requires unsafe and is discouraged.

scenario.question: Your service's JSON marshaling shows up as a CPU hotspot in pprof, dominated by reflect calls. The structs are stable and known at build time. How do you keep the convenience while recovering performance?
scenario.directAnswer: encoding/json uses reflection per call, which is the cost you're seeing. Options, roughly in order: cache decoded type info if rolling your own; switch hot types to code generation (easyjson, ffjson, or json/v2 patterns) that emits static marshal code with no reflection; or implement MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON by hand for the hottest types. Keep reflection-based json for cold paths where developer convenience wins.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Trading reflection's flexibility for generated static code on hot paths.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Reflection resolves field layout at runtime every call; codegen bakes it in at build time.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A generator emits per-type encode/decode functions that access fields by static offset — no dynamic dispatch, far fewer allocations.

scenario.whyImportant: Knowing when to abandon reflection for codegen is a senior-level performance judgment call.
scenario.realWorldExample: High-QPS services replace encoding/json with easyjson for their wire types and cut marshaling CPU dramatically.

followUps.question: What's the downside of generated codecs?
followUps.answer: An extra build step and generated files to keep in sync with the types; flexibility for unknown types is lost.

followUps.question: Can reflection be made faster without codegen?
followUps.answer: Cache reflect.Type metadata so you don't re-walk the type each call; this helps but won't match generated static code.

coding.question: Implement `func StructToMap(v interface{}) map[string]interface{}` that turns a struct (or pointer to one) into a map keyed by the json tag (falling back to the field name), skipping unexported fields.
coding.thoughtProcess: Normalize a pointer to its element with Elem. Confirm it's a struct. Iterate fields; skip unexported ones using PkgPath != "". Prefer the json tag's name part; fall back to the field name. Use Value.Field(i).Interface() to extract the concrete value into the map.
coding.lineByLine: We accept either a struct or *struct, normalizing with Elem. We bail out gracefully on non-structs. PkgPath != "" identifies unexported fields, which we skip (Interface() would panic on them). We read the json tag and strip everything after the first comma to get just the key, falling back to the field name. Field(i).Interface() converts each reflect.Value back to a plain interface{} for the map.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(number of exported fields) for the map.

followUps.question: How would you handle nested structs?
followUps.answer: Recurse: if a field's Kind is Struct (and not a special type like time.Time), call StructToMap on its Interface().

followUps.question: Why check PkgPath instead of name casing?
followUps.answer: PkgPath is the canonical, reliable signal the runtime uses for export status; it's non-empty exactly for unexported fields.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Confine reflection to library boundaries (serialization, config, validation) and present a typed API to the rest of the codebase. Cache reflect.Type metadata per type so you don't re-walk structures on every call.
productionDeepDive.performance: Reflection is roughly an order of magnitude slower than static access and allocates more. For hot paths, cache type info or move to code generation (easyjson and friends); reserve reflection for cold, convenience paths.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: reflect.Type values are immutable and safe to share/cache across goroutines; reflect.Value handles wrap data and must be synchronized like the underlying value. Don't mutate a shared struct via reflection without a lock.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Reflective code fails at runtime with panics (wrong Kind, unsettable value, unexported field). Guard with Kind checks and CanSet(), recover at boundaries, and test every type path — the compiler can't help you here.
productionDeepDive.observability: When reflection shows up in CPU/alloc profiles (reflect.Value.* frames), that's your cue to cache type info or switch to codegen; instrument marshal/unmarshal latency per type.
productionDeepDive.security: Reflection can read fields a caller 'shouldn't' touch and, with unsafe, even unexported ones — be deliberate about what reflective decoders accept, and validate inputs to avoid mapping attacker-controlled keys onto sensitive fields.

caseStudies.problem: Marshal/unmarshal arbitrary user types without per-type code.
caseStudies.solution: Reflect over fields and json tags at runtime, caching type info.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Great ergonomics, but reflection cost and runtime errors instead of compile-time ones.
caseStudies.lessons: Reflection trades speed and compile-time safety for generality — cache and, on hot paths, generate.

caseStudies.problem: Map database rows to arbitrary Go structs.
caseStudies.solution: Reflect over struct fields/tags to build column mappings.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Flexible ORM ergonomics vs. reflection overhead and surprising runtime behavior.
caseStudies.lessons: Reflective ORMs are productive but benefit from caching and explicit field tagging for predictability.

keyTakeaways: Reflection inspects/modifies values whose types aren't known at compile time, working on the (type, value) pair inside an interface.
reflect.Type answers 'what is it?' and reflect.Value holds the data; Kind is the underlying category, Type is the specific named type.
You can only Set an addressable, exported value: use reflect.ValueOf(&x).Elem() and guard with CanSet().
Reflection is powerful but slow and panics at runtime — confine it to libraries, cache type info, and prefer codegen on hot paths.
